title: Freelance Weekly Admin System Kit
description: One admin hour a week that keeps invoices out, payments chased, leads followed up and next week planned. A six-block weekly checklist that protects your cash first, a 45-minute monthly close, a quarterly review with client scorecard, a full worked example with real-looking numbers, a setup guide, a weekly scorecard, 32 recurring admin tasks and a subscription audit.

files.01-weekly-admin-hour.md:
# 1. The Weekly Admin Hour

Sixty minutes, six blocks, always in this order. Set a timer for each block. If a block runs long, finish the item you're on and move on. Anything left goes on next week's list.

Print this page or copy it into your notes app. Work through it top to bottom.

---

## Block 1: Money in (15 minutes)

This is the most important block. Do it first, every time.

**Send invoices**
- [ ] List every piece of work finished since last week's admin hour.
- [ ] For each one, check: has it been invoiced? If not, send the invoice now.
- [ ] Check retainers and recurring work: are any due to be invoiced this week?
- [ ] Check milestones: did any project hit a payment milestone (deposit, midpoint, delivery)?
- [ ] Add any billable extras from the week (extra hours, approved changes, expenses you can pass on).

**Chase overdue invoices**
- [ ] Open your list of unpaid invoices. Sort by due date.
- [ ] For each overdue invoice, send the next reminder in your sequence:

| Days overdue | Action |
|---|---|
| 1-3 | Friendly reminder: "Just a note that invoice [number] was due on [date]. Here it is again in case it got lost." |
| 7 | Second reminder, with the invoice attached and a request for an expected payment date |
| 14 | Short, firmer email; consider pausing new work until payment arrives |
| 30+ | Phone call or formal final notice, following your contract terms |

- [ ] Note any payment that has arrived and mark it paid.

**Quick check**
- [ ] Total unpaid: $______
- [ ] Of which overdue: $______

---

## Block 2: Money out (5 minutes)

- [ ] Save any receipts from this week into your receipts folder, named clearly (date, supplier, amount).
- [ ] Check for bills or subscriptions due in the next 7 days. Is there enough in the account?
- [ ] Note any unusual or unexpected charges to look into (don't investigate now unless it's quick).

---

## Block 3: Pipeline (15 minutes)

Work you win next month depends on what you do this week.

- [ ] Review every open lead and proposal. For each one: what's the next step, and is it overdue?
- [ ] Send follow-ups on any proposal that's had no reply for 5+ working days. A simple one: "Hi [Name], just checking whether you had any questions about the proposal. Happy to adjust anything."
- [ ] Reply to any new enquiries you haven't answered yet.
- [ ] Do one outreach action, even if you're busy: one past-client check-in, one referral ask, one pitch, or one piece of public work shared.
- [ ] Check how full the next four weeks are. Write it down as a rough percentage of capacity.

**Quick check**
- [ ] Open proposals: ______ (value: $______)
- [ ] Next four weeks booked: ______%

---

## Block 4: Clients and projects (10 minutes)

- [ ] For each active project: is it on track? If not, has the client been told?
- [ ] Send any status updates that are due. Two or three lines is enough: done this week, coming next week, anything you need from them.
- [ ] Check for anything waiting on the client (feedback, content, access, approvals). Send one polite nudge per blocked item.
- [ ] Check for any deadlines in the next two weeks that you haven't planned time for.

---

## Block 5: Plan next week (10 minutes)

- [ ] Look at next week's calendar. Block time for each project deliverable.
- [ ] Put your three most important tasks for next week at the top of your list.
- [ ] Schedule next week's admin hour if it's not already a repeating event.
- [ ] Note anything from this hour that needs more than 10 minutes. Give it a time slot.

---

## Block 6: Close (5 minutes)

- [ ] Fill in this week's row in `weekly-scorecard.csv`.
- [ ] Clear your desktop and downloads folder of files from the week (file or delete).
- [ ] Inbox: anything still unread from clients? Reply or schedule a time to reply.
- [ ] If it's the last admin hour of the month, go to `02-monthly-close.md` now.

---

## If you only have 20 minutes

Some weeks are packed. Do these four things and stop:

1. Send any unsent invoices.
2. Send reminders on overdue invoices.
3. Reply to new enquiries.
4. Fill in the scorecard.

These protect your cash and your pipeline. Everything else can wait a week.

## If you have nothing to do

On a quiet week the hour might take 15 minutes. Use the spare time for one improvement:

- Write or update one email template you keep rewriting
- Update your portfolio with a recent project
- Clean up one folder
- Read through last month's scorecard rows and spot one trend
files.02-monthly-close.md:
# 2. The Monthly Close

Forty-five minutes on top of your last weekly admin hour of the month. The goal: know exactly how the month went, set money aside, and start next month clean.

---

## Part 1: Reconcile (15 minutes)

- [ ] Download or open your business bank statement for the month.
- [ ] Match every payment received to an invoice. Mark each invoice paid.
- [ ] Match every business expense to a receipt. Note any missing receipts and find them now, or note why they're missing.
- [ ] Note any personal spending that went through the business account, or business spending that went through a personal account, so it can be recorded properly.
- [ ] Check that every invoice you sent this month appears in your income records.

## Part 2: Know your numbers (10 minutes)

Fill this in each month. Keep a running copy so you can compare months.

| Number | This month | Last month |
|---|---|---|
| Invoiced (work billed this month) | | |
| Received (money actually paid in) | | |
| Business expenses | | |
| Profit (received minus expenses) | | |
| Unpaid at month end | | |
| Of which overdue | | |
| Hours worked on client projects (if you track them) | | |
| Effective hourly rate (received divided by total hours worked, including admin) | | |
| Largest client's share of income | | |

**Three questions to answer in one line each:**
1. What went better than last month?
2. What went worse?
3. What's one thing I'll do differently next month?

## Part 3: Set money aside (5 minutes)

Freelancers usually have to set aside money for tax because no employer is doing it for them. The right percentage depends on where you live, your income and your expenses, so check with an accountant or your local tax authority. Once you know your percentage:

- [ ] Work out this month's set-aside: money received x your percentage.
- [ ] Move it to a separate savings account now.
- [ ] If you keep a buffer or "pay yourself" account, move this month's amount too.

### Example

Received this month: $5,200. Percentage set by an accountant: 25%.
Set-aside: $5,200 x 0.25 = $1,300, moved to the tax account on the last working day.

## Part 4: Subscriptions and tools (5 minutes)

- [ ] Open `subscription-audit.csv`. Add any new subscriptions.
- [ ] Check anything renewing next month. Still using it? If not, cancel before it renews.
- [ ] Look for duplicates (two tools that do the same job).

## Part 5: Housekeeping (10 minutes)

- [ ] Back up client files and your business records. Check that the backup actually opened, at least once a quarter.
- [ ] Archive finished projects into a "Completed" folder.
- [ ] Update your portfolio list: note any finished project worth adding later, and whether you need client permission.
- [ ] Ask for a testimonial from any client whose project finished well this month.
- [ ] Check upcoming holidays or time off. Have clients been told?
- [ ] Note any rate changes, contract renewals or retainer reviews coming up next month.

## When the month went badly

If income is down or overdue invoices are up, don't skip the close. That's when it matters most. Look for one cause you can act on:

| What you see | Likely cause | First thing to try |
|---|---|---|
| Invoiced is high, received is low | Slow payers or long payment terms | Shorter terms or deposits on new work; firmer reminder sequence |
| Invoiced is low | Not enough booked work, or work not invoiced yet | Check for unsent invoices; spend more of Block 3 on outreach |
| Expenses are creeping up | Subscriptions or tools added and forgotten | Subscription audit; cancel one tool |
| Effective hourly rate is falling | Admin and unbilled extras growing, or rates too low | Track time for two weeks; quote extras; review rates in the quarterly review |
| One client is more than half your income | Concentration risk | Make pipeline building a weekly priority until it drops |
files.03-quarterly-review.md:
# 3. The Quarterly Review

Ninety minutes every three months. Book it as a separate session, ideally away from your usual desk. The weekly hour keeps things running. This review decides what to change.

Bring: your last 13 weeks of `weekly-scorecard.csv`, your three monthly close tables, and your client list.

---

## Part 1: Look back (30 minutes)

### Your numbers for the quarter

| Number | This quarter | Last quarter |
|---|---|---|
| Total received | | |
| Total expenses | | |
| Profit | | |
| Average days to get paid | | |
| Number of active clients | | |
| Number of new clients | | |
| Proposals sent | | |
| Proposals won | | |
| Win rate (won divided by sent) | | |
| Weeks you did the admin hour (out of 13) | | |

### Client scorecard

Rate each client from 1 (poor) to 3 (great) on four things:

| Client | Pays well | Pays on time | Good to work with | Leads to more work | Total (out of 12) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | | | | | |
| | | | | | |
| | | | | | |
| | | | | | |

- **10-12:** Look after them. Could you do more for them?
- **7-9:** Fine. Is there one thing that would move them up a band?
- **4-6:** Review. Raise rates, change terms, or plan to replace this income.

### What happened

Answer in a sentence or two each:
1. What was my best project this quarter, and why?
2. What was my worst project, and what caused it?
3. Where did I lose the most time?
4. What did I say yes to that I should have said no to?

## Part 2: Pricing (20 minutes)

- [ ] When did you last raise your rates? If it's been more than 12 months, put a rate review on your list.
- [ ] Compare your effective hourly rate (from your monthly closes) to the rate you think you charge. A gap usually means unbilled time.
- [ ] Is any client or service well below your current rates? Decide: raise, repackage or phase out.
- [ ] Are you regularly fully booked? Being full for most of the quarter is often a sign your prices can go up.

## Part 3: Pipeline and clients (20 minutes)

- [ ] Where did your new clients come from this quarter? (referrals, past clients, outreach, platforms, word of mouth)
- [ ] Which source gave the best clients, not just the most? Plan to do more of that.
- [ ] Is your largest client more than 40-50% of your income? If so, set a pipeline goal for next quarter.
- [ ] List three past clients to check in with next quarter.
- [ ] List one new kind of client or project you'd like more of.

## Part 4: Plan next quarter (20 minutes)

Pick no more than three goals. Make each one specific and measurable.

| Goal | Measure | First step | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. | | | |
| 2. | | | |
| 3. | | | |

### Example goals

- Get average days-to-paid under 25 by asking for 50% deposits on all new projects.
- Win two new clients from referrals by asking every happy client at project end.
- Raise rates by 10% for new clients from the first of next month.
- Reduce the largest client from 55% to under 45% of income.

### Admin system check

- [ ] Did the weekly hour happen at least 10 weeks out of 13? If not, move it to a better time slot.
- [ ] Which block do you always rush or skip? Make it shorter, or move it earlier.
- [ ] Add or remove anything from `recurring-admin-tasks.csv`.
- [ ] Book next quarter's review now.
files.04-worked-example.md:
# 4. Worked Example

Jordan is a freelance copywriter with five active clients. Before using this system, Jordan did admin "whenever", usually late at night, and regularly found invoices that had never been sent.

Jordan's admin hour is **Friday, 10:00 to 11:00**. This is the last Friday of October, so it's also the monthly close.

All names and figures are made up for illustration.

---

## The weekly admin hour

### Block 1: Money in (10:00-10:15)

**Work finished since last Friday:**
- Website copy for a software startup: final draft approved on Wednesday. That triggers the delivery milestone.
- Two hours of extra edits for a local dental practice, approved by email on Monday.
- The garden centre retainer is due to be invoiced on the 1st, so it goes out today, dated 1 November.

**Invoices sent:**

| Client | What | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| Software startup | Website copy, final milestone (50%) | $1,200 |
| Garden centre | November retainer | $800 |
| Dental practice | 2 hours extra edits at $75 | $150 |
| **Total** | | **$2,150** |

Jordan almost forgot the dental practice edits. They were approved in an email thread, not in the project tracker. The "billable extras" check caught them.

**Overdue invoices:**

| Invoice | Client | Amount | Days overdue | Action today |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1041 | Dental practice | $600 | 9 | Second reminder, asked for an expected payment date |
| 1043 | Accountancy firm | $450 | 3 | Friendly reminder with invoice attached |

**Payments received:** $900 from a charity client. Marked paid.

**Quick check:** Total unpaid $3,200. Overdue $1,050.

### Block 2: Money out (10:15-10:20)

- Saved three receipts: a stock photo licence, a co-working day pass and a book.
- A writing software subscription ($29) renews on Tuesday. Still used daily. Keep.
- Nothing unusual on the account.

### Block 3: Pipeline (10:20-10:35)

**Open proposals:**

| Prospect | Value | Sent | Status | Next step |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Online shop (product descriptions) | $1,800 | 6 working days ago | No reply | Follow-up sent today |
| Recruitment agency (website refresh) | $2,400 | 3 working days ago | Questions answered | Wait until next Friday |
| Café (menu and social bios) | $650 | Yesterday | New | Wait |

- Replied to one new enquiry from a yoga studio; offered two call times next week.
- Outreach: sent a short check-in to a past client from the spring, asking how the new website was performing.
- Next four weeks: about 70% booked.

**Quick check:** Three open proposals worth $4,850. 70% booked.

### Block 4: Clients and projects (10:35-10:45)

- Software startup: on track. Sent a short update.
- Garden centre: waiting on photos for the November newsletter. Sent one polite nudge.
- Dental practice: no issues, apart from the overdue invoice (handled in Block 1).
- Noticed the recruitment agency project, if won, would start the same week as a big garden centre campaign. Made a note to propose a start date one week later.

### Block 5: Plan next week (10:45-10:55)

Top three for next week:
1. Garden centre newsletter (needs photos by Tuesday)
2. Software startup: blog post outlines
3. Yoga studio discovery call

Blocked time on the calendar for each. Next Friday's admin hour is already a repeating event.

### Block 6: Close (10:55-11:00)

Filled in the scorecard row for the week ending 30 October. Cleared the downloads folder. It's the last Friday of the month, so on to the monthly close.

---

## The monthly close (11:00-11:45)

### Reconcile

All four October payments matched invoices. One receipt was missing (a train ticket to a client workshop). Jordan found it in an email and saved it.

### October numbers

| Number | October | September |
|---|---|---|
| Invoiced | $5,650 | $4,900 |
| Received | $5,200 | $4,300 |
| Business expenses | $410 | $385 |
| Profit | $4,790 | $3,915 |
| Unpaid at month end | $3,200 | $2,750 |
| Of which overdue | $1,050 | $1,600 |
| Hours on client projects | 96 | 90 |
| Total hours worked, including admin | 118 | 115 |
| Effective hourly rate | $44.07 | $37.39 |
| Largest client's share of income | 38% | 44% |

Effective hourly rate = received divided by total hours. October: $5,200 / 118 = $44.07.

**Three questions:**
1. Better: overdue money is down by a third, because reminders now go out every Friday instead of "when I remember".
2. Worse: still 22 hours of non-billable time. Mostly admin and unpaid calls.
3. Next month: send a short quote for every extra over 20 minutes, instead of doing it and hoping to bill it later.

### Set money aside

Jordan's accountant suggested setting aside 25% of money received.
$5,200 x 0.25 = **$1,300**, moved to the tax savings account.

### Subscriptions

The audit found two design tools used for making social graphics. Jordan kept one and cancelled the other, saving $15 a month ($180 a year).

### Housekeeping

- Backed up all client folders; opened one file from the backup to check it worked.
- Archived two finished projects.
- Asked the charity client for a testimonial, as their project wrapped up well.
- Noted: garden centre retainer is up for review in December. Add a rate review to November's to-do list.

---

## What changed after three months

By the end of January, Jordan had done the admin hour 12 weeks out of 13. Compared with the three months before starting:

- Average days to get paid fell from 41 to 27.
- Unsent invoices found during the hour: four in the first month, one in the second, none in the third.
- Late-night admin sessions went from "most weeks" to almost none.

These are illustrative figures. Your results will depend on your clients, your terms and how consistently you run the hour.
files.05-setup-guide.md:
# 5. Setup Guide

Forty-five minutes, once. After this, the system runs on a calendar reminder and a checklist.

## Step 1: Choose your admin hour (5 minutes)

Pick a fixed, weekly 60-minute slot. Good slots share three things:

- **Low energy for creative work** but enough focus for numbers. For many people that's Friday morning or Monday after lunch.
- **Early enough in the week to act on what you find.** Friday works well because invoices go out before the weekend and you plan next week with fresh information. Monday works if you prefer to start the week with a clear picture.
- **Rarely clashes with client calls.** Block it as busy so booking tools never offer it.

My admin hour: ______________ (day) at ______________ (time)

Create a repeating calendar event. Paste the six block names into the event description, so the checklist is in front of you when it starts.

Also create:
- A repeating event for the **monthly close** (45 minutes straight after your last admin hour of each month).
- A repeating event for the **quarterly review** (90 minutes, in the first two weeks after each quarter ends).

## Step 2: Set up your folders (10 minutes)

A simple structure that works for most freelancers:

```
Business/
  Admin/
    weekly-scorecard.csv
    recurring-admin-tasks.csv
    subscription-audit.csv
  Clients/
    Client name/
      Active/
      Completed/
  Finance/
    Invoices/2026/
    Receipts/2026/
    Monthly closes/
  Templates/
```

Name receipt files the same way every time, for example `2026-10-14 supplier 29.00.pdf`. A consistent name means you can find anything by searching, without opening files.

## Step 3: List your open money and work (15 minutes)

You can't run Block 1 without knowing what's outstanding. Make three quick lists:

1. **Every unpaid invoice**: number, client, amount, due date.
2. **Every open proposal or lead**: who, value, date sent, next step.
3. **Every active project**: client, next deadline, anything you're waiting on.

Keep them wherever you'll actually look: a spreadsheet, your invoicing tool, a notes page. The format matters less than keeping them in one place.

## Step 4: Set up the CSV files (10 minutes)

- **`weekly-scorecard.csv`:** delete the example rows and add a row for this week.
- **`recurring-admin-tasks.csv`:** read through the list. Delete anything that doesn't apply to you. Add anything missing (for example, a monthly report you send to a retainer client).
- **`subscription-audit.csv`:** go through last month's bank statement and list every business subscription.

## Step 5: Run your first admin hour (it may take longer)

Your first one or two admin hours may take 90 minutes, because you'll find backlogs: an unsent invoice, a proposal nobody followed up, a pile of receipts. That's normal. By week three, most people are inside 60 minutes.

---

## Common ways it breaks, and fixes

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| "I keep skipping it when I'm busy." | Use the 20-minute version on busy weeks (bottom of file 01). The habit matters more than doing every box. |
| "A client always books calls in my admin slot." | Move the hour to a time they never book, or block it as busy so it's not offered. |
| "I start fixing things and run out of time." | Use a timer for each block. Anything over 10 minutes goes on next week's list. |
| "I don't know what to put in the scorecard." | Start with just three numbers: invoiced, received, overdue. Add the rest after a month. |
| "My invoices live in different places." | Pick one place to list unpaid invoices, even if they're sent from different tools. |
| "I forget the monthly close." | Make it a separate repeating calendar event, not a mental note. |
| "The checklist doesn't fit my work." | Edit it. Delete lines that never apply; add the ones you keep remembering at 11pm. |

## Making it stick

- **Pair it with something you enjoy:** a favourite coffee, a playlist, working from a café.
- **Count streaks:** mark each completed week on a calendar. Aim for 10 out of 13 weeks per quarter.
- **Notice the payoff:** after a month, compare your overdue total and unsent invoices to where you started.
files.README.md:
# Freelance Weekly Admin System Kit

One admin hour a week that keeps invoices out, payments chased, leads followed up and next week planned, so business admin stops leaking into every evening.

Most freelancers don't have a money problem or a client problem. They have a "the invoice didn't get sent for three weeks" problem. This kit gives you a fixed routine: one hour every week, a short monthly close and a quarterly review. Each has a checklist you work through in order, so you don't have to remember anything.

Plan on 45 minutes to set up, then 60 minutes a week.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for |
|---|---|
| 01-weekly-admin-hour.md | The core routine: a 60-minute checklist in six blocks, in the order that protects your cash first |
| 02-monthly-close.md | A 45-minute end-of-month checklist: money, numbers, subscriptions, backups |
| 03-quarterly-review.md | A 90-minute review every three months: clients, pricing, pipeline and what to change |
| 04-worked-example.md | One real-feeling week and month for a freelance copywriter, start to finish |
| 05-setup-guide.md | How to set up the system in 45 minutes, plus fixes for the most common ways it breaks |
| weekly-scorecard.csv | Eight numbers to record each week, with example rows |
| recurring-admin-tasks.csv | 32 recurring admin tasks with frequency, time needed and where each one lives in the routine |
| subscription-audit.csv | A list of your business subscriptions with cost, renewal date and keep or cancel decision |

## How to use it

1. **Set up (45 minutes).** Follow `05-setup-guide.md`. Choose your admin hour, set a repeating calendar block and set up the scorecard.
2. **Every week (60 minutes).** Work through `01-weekly-admin-hour.md` from top to bottom. Record your numbers in `weekly-scorecard.csv`.
3. **Every month (45 minutes).** On your last admin hour of the month, add `02-monthly-close.md`.
4. **Every quarter (90 minutes).** Book a separate session for `03-quarterly-review.md`.

## Why the order matters

The weekly checklist starts with money coming in, because that's the task with the highest cost when it slips. A late invoice means late payment, and the delay compounds: an invoice sent two weeks late on 30-day terms means waiting six weeks or more for money you earned. If your hour gets cut short, you've still done the part that matters most.

## Ground rules

- **Same time every week.** A fixed slot beats "when I have a quiet moment". Quiet moments don't come.
- **Do it even when it's quiet.** A five-minute admin hour on a slow week still counts. The habit is the point.
- **Don't fix things during the hour, note them.** If a task will take more than 10 minutes, put it on next week's to-do list and keep moving.
- **Keep the scorecard honest.** Write down the real numbers, not the ones you hoped for. Trends are only useful if they're true.

This kit gives general business guidance, not tax, legal or accounting advice. Tax set-aside amounts and record-keeping rules depend on where you live. Check with a qualified accountant or your local tax authority.
